notes:
I've put together notes on all twelve verses. My searches turned up nothing from the Lutheran, Anglican, NET Bible notes or Bible Odyssey sites, and nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching about this chapter, so those are left out. The real disagreements I found come up at v. 5, v. 9 and v. 11.

**v. 1**
- **Who's writing:** Silvanus (Silas) was Paul's companion on his second missionary journey and was with him when he first came to Thessalonica. Timothy was a trusted helper whom Paul had sent to the church once before. Both had helped write 1 Thessalonians too. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-thessalonians-1/
- **"Church":** The Greek word first meant an "assembly." It came to mean an organised worshipping body, whether or not it was gathered at the moment. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ctf/2-thessalonians-1.html
- **Repeated wording:** Matthew Henry notes that Paul reuses phrases from his first letter. He takes this to show that preachers should care more about truth and usefulness than about variety or fine style. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Th/2Th_001.cfm

**v. 2**
- **Father and Son as one source:** Guzik quotes Bicknell (via Leon Morris): the Greek treats the Father and Christ as a single source of grace. It is striking that, this early, the Son is placed beside the Father without any explanation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-thessalonians-1/
- **Why Paul starts with grace (Chrysostom, early Church Father):** Paul opens with grace to soften his readers before any rebuke. Remembering the grace that saved them from the greater evil should keep them from despairing in smaller troubles. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/chrysostom/2_thessalonians/1.htm

**v. 3**
- **Thanks as a duty:** For Paul, thanking God was an obligation ("bound") and fitting. Morris suggests the Thessalonians had protested that they didn't deserve the praise in the first letter, and Paul insists it wasn't overstated. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-thessalonians-1/
- **The verb for "growing":** It appears nowhere else in Scripture. It means faith increasing beyond measure, and its present tense means the growth is still going on. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-thessalonians-1-commentary
- **"Increasing" love:** Utley says the image is of swelling floodwaters. Praising their love for one another mattered because the church had fellowship problems. https://bible.org/seriespage/2-thessalonians-1
- **Wesley (Methodist):** Paul folds his praise of people into praise of God. "Aboundeth" is like water spilling over its banks and still rising. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-second-epistle-to-the-thessalonians/
- **Matthew Henry:** Where grace is real, it grows. We depend on God's grace for growth just as much as for the first work of grace. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Th/2Th_001.cfm
- **Chrysostom:** He calls the verse a sign of great humility. If others thank God first for our good deeds, we should do so even more. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/chrysostom/2_thessalonians/1.htm

**v. 4**
- **"Endure":** Hiebert pictures believers holding themselves upright and firm under suffering for their faith. "Persecutions" and "afflictions" are both plural, meaning the troubles were many and varied. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-thessalonians-1-commentary
- **Why it was remarkable:** Chrysostom notes these were poor day-labourers who took on hostility from the city's rulers, at a time when no king or governor was a believer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/chrysostom/2_thessalonians/1.htm

**v. 5** (a debated verse)
- **What counts as the "evidence"?**
  - **Their endurance, not the suffering itself:** Ryrie says the proof is their faith and steadiness under persecution. The ESV Study Bible says that because God is giving them grace to endure, He is clearly on their side. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-thessalonians-1-commentary
  - **The persecution itself:** Ellicott says the sign is mainly the fact that they were persecuted. It shows how God's fair judgment will go on the last day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_thessalonians/1-5.htm
- **Is the judgment present or future?**
  - **Present and purifying:** Guzik sees God's judgment already at work, "beginning at the house of God" (1 Peter 4:17). Persecution is a refiner's fire. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-thessalonians-1/
  - **Future:** Matthew Poole and the Pulpit Commentary reject the present-discipline reading. They say the righteous suffering while the wicked go unpunished proves a final judgment must come to set things right. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_thessalonians/1-5.htm
- **"Counted worthy": merit or grace?**
  - **Reformed and evangelical:** Ryrie says the verb means "declare worthy," not "make worthy," like "justify." Morris says Paul's word choice rules out human merit. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-thessalonians-1-commentary
  - **Ligonier (Reformed):** It is right for God to count us worthy because Christ's worth is credited to us ("imputed"). https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/the-righteous-judgment-of-god
  - **Guzik:** He likewise reads it as Christ's worthiness credited to believers. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-thessalonians-1/
  - **Barnes:** Christians don't earn heaven by suffering. It shows they have a character fit for heaven. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_thessalonians/1-5.htm
  - **Other voices on the same page:** The Pulpit Commentary adds that grace doesn't cancel God's justice, and the righteous will be rewarded for faith and patience. Meyer goes further: their endurance made them worthy of a share in the kingdom. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_thessalonians/1-5.htm
  - **Chrysostom (Catholic/Orthodox):** God's justice shows when He crowns the sufferers and punishes the persecutors. They are crowned for their own labours, in proportion to their righteousness. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23052.htm

**v. 6**
- **"After all" ("if so be"):** Chrysostom says it means "because" and expresses certainty, not doubt. If repaying evil is just among humans, it is even more so with God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/chrysostom/2_thessalonians/1.htm
- **Wesley:** It is right with God, whatever people think, to shift the pressure from the believers onto their persecutors. He links this to a massacre of Jews at Passover around that time. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-second-epistle-to-the-thessalonians/
- **Guzik:** The verse is like the Psalms that ask for judgment on enemies: it hands judgment over to God instead of taking revenge. All evil will be dealt with, either at the cross or in hell. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-thessalonians-1/
- **Application:** Christians are not to avenge wrongs themselves; God will. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ctf/2-thessalonians-1.html

**v. 7**
- **"Relief" (or "rest"):** In Greek it is a noun meaning relaxation or ease. The persecutors are repaid with affliction; the persecuted are repaid with rest. That rest comes in the next world, not this one. https://biblehub.com/2_thessalonians/1-7.htm
- **The angels:** They come with Christ both to carry out judgment and to gather the redeemed (Matthew 24:31). https://biblehub.com/2_thessalonians/1-7.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** God's people will have rest from sin and sorrow, and it will far outweigh their present troubles. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Th/2Th_001.cfm

**v. 8**
- **"Vengeance":** Morris (quoted by Guzik) says the word carries no vindictiveness. It shares a root with "righteous" in vv. 5–6 and means firm, steady justice. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-thessalonians-1/
- **One group or two?**
  - **Wesley:** "Who know not God" means pagans still in ignorance. "Who obey not" refers mainly to Jews who had heard the gospel. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-second-epistle-to-the-thessalonians/
  - **Utley:** He notes that some commentators read it this way. https://bible.org/seriespage/2-thessalonians-1
- **Chrysostom:** Paul says "those who do not obey," not "those who afflict you." So punishment is required for God's own sake, and persecutors will suffer even more. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/chrysostom/2_thessalonians/1.htm
- **Bible.org (Steven Cole):** Someone who claims Jesus as Savior but won't submit to Him as Lord makes a questionable claim. Those who live in disobedience don't know Him. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-2-eternal-destruction-or-eternal-glory-2-thessalonians-16-10

**v. 9** (the most debated verse)
- **Traditional view, endless conscious punishment:**
  - **Packer (The Gospel Coalition):** "Separated from the presence of the Lord" rules out extinction, because only those who exist can be shut out. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/j-i-packer-on-why-annihilationism-is-wrong/
  - **Barnes:** The word for "destruction" doesn't mean annihilation. The soul is ruined as to the purposes it was made for, yet goes on existing. https://studylight.org/commentary/2-thessalonians/1-9.html
  - **Wesley (Methodist):** Their sin never ends, so neither does their punishment. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-second-epistle-to-the-thessalonians/
  - **Matthew Henry:** They will be "always dying, and yet never die." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Th/2Th_001.cfm
  - **Assemblies of God (Pentecostal):** Its position paper says annihilationism errs by making death permanent. It reads the verse as final, eternal separation from God. https://ag.org/Beliefs/Position-Papers/Final-Judgment
- **What annihilationists argue (as these sites describe them):**
  - Destruction is final, the punished cease to exist, and endless torment wouldn't fit God's love and justice. https://biblehub.com/q/what_is_annihilationism.htm
  - The punishment is called eternal because its result is permanent. https://www.monergism.com/annihilationism
  - Precept Austin notes that respected theologians such as John Stott argued against eternal punishment, while Wiersbe called the alternatives false. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-thessalonians-1-commentary
- **Guzik:** The worst of hell is not the fire but being cut off from everything good in God's presence. Only His holy justice remains. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-thessalonians-1/

**v. 10**
- **"Regarded with wonder by all who have believed":** Chrysostom reads "in" as "through." God's power is seen when He brings people who were pitied and suffering into great glory. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/chrysostom/2_thessalonians/1.htm
- **Wesley:** Christ's glory will shine in His saints. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-second-epistle-to-the-thessalonians/
- **Guzik:** What divides those headed for judgment from those headed for glory is believing the simple gospel Paul preached. He quotes Spurgeon: every saint will be a wonder even to himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-thessalonians-1/
- **Ray Stedman:** Believers are glorified not for living a decent life but for trusting that Another died in their place. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-thessalonians-1-commentary

**v. 11** (a debated verse)
- **"Count" or "make" worthy?**
  - **Matthew Henry:** The verb could also be read "make you worthy." He understands it as God carrying on His work of grace in them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Th/2Th_001.cfm
  - **Wesley (Methodist/Holiness):** "All the good pleasure of his goodness" means nothing less than perfect holiness. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-second-epistle-to-the-thessalonians/
  - **Chrysostom:** Some who are called don't stay in their calling, like the guest without wedding clothes who was thrown out. That's why Paul prays God will fulfil their good desire. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/chrysostom/2_thessalonians/1.htm
- **Guzik:** Living worthy of the call means showing God's goodness and doing the work of faith with power. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-thessalonians-1/

**v. 12**
- **Guzik:** "The name" stands for Christ's character, and believers are glorified "in Him" when He is their only source of glory. All this happens by grace, which works in us and moves our will to cooperate. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-thessalonians-1/
- **Chrysostom:** Christ is glorified in us when we put nothing before Him and his strength keeps us from giving way under trouble. Onlookers praise Him for strengthening us. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/chrysostom/2_thessalonians/1.htm
- **Wesley:** The Lord's love and power are gloriously displayed in believers. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-second-epistle-to-the-thessalonians/
- **Translation note:** Most versions (KJV, NASB) have "our God and the Lord Jesus Christ." The International Standard Version has "our God and Lord, Jesus, the Messiah," which calls Jesus God. I couldn't find a commentary explaining the difference. https://biblehub.com/interlinear/2_thessalonians/1-12.htm
